newsitem.title: INDIA: BPL Cellular withdraws India's first ADR issue.
newsitem.headline: BPL Cellular withdraws India's first ADR issue.

text.p: Fledgling Indian telecom firm BPL Cellular said on Thursday it was withdrawing its $200 million issue of American Depositary Receipts (ADR) -- the country's first U.S. offering.
BPL Cellular said in a statement it was forced to withdraw the issue due to poor sentiment for India. The announcement came after repeated delays in the pricing of the issue.

"... given the prevailing negative sentiments in the international markets towards Indian stocks it is quite likely that the stock would have been priced at a substantial discount to its true value and in addition, with a likelihood of performing poorly in the aftermarket," the firm said in a statement.
The firm said it was working with global co-ordinator Morgan Stanley to arrange alternate financing for its projects.
Investment banking sources said BPL's alternate finance arrangements could include a private placement. Morgan Stanley officials were not immediately available for comment.
A source close to the issue said the firm had received a good response but was unable to get its indicative pricing of $15-$17 an ADR.
"We had a good response as far as the book was concerned but we were not sure whether they were long-term investors," the source told Reuters.
"Besides we were not sure that the price being asked for was representative of the real price," he said.
He said the company had received bids $10 and upwards.
But most investment bankers and fund managers said bids were in the range of $8 to $10 with stray bids as low as $5.

Indian firms have traditionally raised international equity through Global Depositary Receipts (GDRs) but fledgling telecom firms -- lured by the promise of access to the world's largest capital market -- are opting to raise equity by issuing ADRs.

Aggressive marketing by American investment banks promising greater access to investors and the prestige of a Nasdaq listing have made some firms like BPL Cellular, Bharati Televentures and Hutchison Max opt for ADRs.
"BPL was a do-able deal if they had started at a $100 million issue and priced it at $10," said a director at a European investment bank.
"But once you misjudge the market the initiative is totally lost," he said.
An investment banker closely associated with a forthcoming ADR issue by an Indian company said the withdrawal would impact forthcoming issues.
"I don't think they have served the death knell but it's better than being priced and tanking," the banker said.
"Once a deal is so dramatically downsized investors do tend to run scared," he added.
